name: Ulwa
confidence_why: Barlow's 2023 reference grammar (repeating his 2018 dissertation almost word for word) is the only description of Ulwa stress, and it states plainly that stress is not phonemic and falls on either the last or the second-to-last syllable of a word with a slight penultimate preference, which is exactly what the record says; nothing contradicts it, but it is a single first-hand source.

catalog_quote: [Barlow 2023 sec. 4.4, p. 93] Stress in Ulwa is not phonemic. In single-word utterances, disyllabic words may receive stress either on the ultima or on the penult, although there is perhaps a slight preference for penultimate (trochaic) stress. In longer words and phrases, pragmatic factors play a significant role in stress assignment, although there is nevertheless a tendency for stress to fall on alternating syllables. Ulwa may be considered a syllable-timed language. There is no phonemic tone, nor are there other suprasegmental phonemic distinctions found in the language, such as vowel length. ... [sec. 3.1, p. 54] Stress is not phonemic. There is a preference for penultimate stress in polysyllabic words and for alternating stress in longer utterances.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is not phonemic and has no fixed position. In isolated disyllables stress falls on either the final or the penultimate syllable, with only a 'slight preference' for the penult (trochaic). In longer words and phrases placement is driven by pragmatic factors, with a tendency toward alternating (rhythmic) syllables. The language is described as syllable-timed, with no tone and no other suprasegmental contrasts. The 'fixed: penultimate syllable' label is the nearest item on the fixed list and should be read as 'non-contrastive, variable, weak penultimate tendency', not as a rule.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No explicit statement; the only relevant remark is the 'tendency for stress to fall on alternating syllables' in longer words and phrases (p. 70), which implies rhythmic alternation without naming secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions; the source itself frames placement as variable (ultima or penult in disyllables) and pragmatically conditioned in longer words, so no rule with exceptions is stated.
new_statements.identity_note: Barlow 2018 describes the Manu-village dialect of Ulwa as spoken by older speakers (data from three trips to Manu, 2015–2017; p. 2 and §1.5: 'this is, foremost, a grammatical description of the Manu dialect of the Ulwa language as spoken by older speakers'). Ulwa has two major dialects, Manu vs. Maruat–Dimiri–Yaul; Laycock's survey name 'Yaul' (hence the Glottocode yaul1241 and ISO yla) is the name of one village, and Foley 2018 calls the language 'Yaul-Dimiri'. Fewer than 700 speakers, Angoram District, East Sepik.
